sentences.speaker: Anchor
sentences.text: As summers get hotter, more cities are turning to one of the oldest tools there is: trees.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: On a July afternoon, the asphalt on this street can get hot enough to burn bare feet.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Just a few blocks away, under a line of old oaks, it's noticeably cooler.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Researchers call this difference the urban heat island effect.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Pavement and rooftops soak up heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so neighborhoods with little shade can stay warm long after sunset.

sentences.speaker: Planner
sentences.text: We used to think of trees as decoration.

sentences.speaker: Planner
sentences.text: Now we treat them as infrastructure, like pipes or power lines.

sentences.speaker: Planner
sentences.text: A healthy tree canopy cools the street, cleans the air, and honestly, it makes people wanna walk outside.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: But planting is the easy part.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Young trees need water, care, and years of growth before they give real shade, and the neighborhoods that need them most often have the least room for them.

sentences.speaker: Planner
sentences.text: You can't just drop a sapling into a crack in the sidewalk and walk away.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Still, city leaders here say the math is simple.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Every tree that survives is a little shade that didn't exist before.

sentences.speaker: Reporter
sentences.text: Reporting from downtown, I'm Claire Hughes.
